summary: Glendora sits right where the San Gabriel Mountains drop abruptly into the foothill plain, and several of its neighborhoods literally terminate at the mouths of canyons — meaning a resident on the north side can walk from a cul-de-sac onto trails leading into the Angeles National Forest in minutes, an arrangement that feels more like a Colorado front-range town than the eastern San Gabriel Valley. That mountain proximity delivers genuine sunset drama: the western sky lights up over the valley floor while the peaks behind cast long shadows. Daily highs average 76°F with 9.3 hours of sunshine, so the climate is dry, warm, and remarkably consistent, though summer afternoons can trap heat against those north-facing slopes. The town's historic downtown along Route 66 — Glendora Village — offers a walkable strip of independent restaurants and coffee shops, but beyond that corridor the street pattern is car-oriented and typical of postwar suburbia, with limited transit connectivity. At a median household income of roughly $112K and a median home price near $821K, the price-to-income ratio sits around 7.3, steep but noticeably below neighboring foothill cities closer to Pasadena. Most of the employment base lies elsewhere — largely reached via the 210 and 57 freeways — making this firmly a bedroom community, with the tradeoff being that quiet evenings and canyon-edge hiking access come at the cost of a commute that can stretch well past thirty minutes during peak hours.
